title: The Guardian view on events in Ceuta: chaos and tragedy are weaponised by the far right | Editorial
content: Instead of finger-pointing at Spain, mainstream EU leaders should be showing solidarity with its prime minister, Pedro Sánchez At least 72 people are believed to have died late last week, most of them drowned or crushed as they joined tens of thousands of others in attempting to swim from Moroccan waters to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Yet the scale of that human tragedy has barely registered, as Donald Trump has decried an “invasion” while European politicians exploit the crisis to serve their own agendas. If further evidence were needed of the way that the radical right increasingly distorts the terms of the migration debate in the EU, the last few days have furnished it. More needs to be understood about the drivers behind a shocking episode. Misinformation on social media – orchestrated or otherwise – appears to have played a big part, following a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily turned back. Moroccan authorities seemingly did little to prevent the chaotic exodus, which echoed previous smaller incidents and focused international attention on a territory whose sovereignty Rabat contests. If there were online indications that such an incursion was a possibility, no alarm was sounded. The Spanish government, distracted by the need to combat ongoing wildfires, was utterly unprepared. But the vast majority of the 60,000 or so who crossed into Ceuta returned voluntarily across the border within 48 hours, some having aired grievances to reporters at the lack of work, decent wages and prospects available to them at home. The dangerous recklessness of their actions underlined the pressure-cooker levels of frustration beyond Europe’s external borders, particularly among the young. Subsequently, the response of leaders such as Italy’s Giorgia Meloni has been predictable but deeply dispiriting. In a performative overreaction, Ms Meloni sought to demonstrate her hard line on irregular migration by temporarily suspending Rome’s Schengen agreement with Madrid, though Ceuta has never been included in Schengen, and Italy and Spain share no border. Along with Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, she was also among 22 signatories to a letter sent to the European Commission, suggesting that the liberal migration policies of the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – which, again, have no application in Ceuta – are undermining Europe’s security. Such posturing is largely intended for a domestic audience. Mr Merz, for example, faces a major challenge from the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in three imminent state elections, while Ms Meloni is dealing with the emergence of a new party that threatens her own right flank. The zeal of such forces to weaponise the immigration issue was shown by the speed with which the AfD’s leader, Alice Weidel, claimed that the “likely destination” for most of those entering Ceuta was Germany. Hyperbolic rhetoric and finger-pointing will only undermine solidarity between European nations, and hamper attempts to deal effectively with the challenges of migration. It is impossible to cross from Ceuta into mainland Spain and the Schengen zone without passing through a checkpoint. It is also worth noting that the number of irregular border crossings into Europe in fact declined by 40% in the first half of 2026 compared with last year, partly as a result of better-coordinated preventive strategies. Instead of rounding on Mr Sánchez, mainstream European leaders should be pledging their cooperation in helping Spain to minimise the possibility of such a tragic incident ever happening again. centralIdea: The editorial criticizes far-right European politicians for weaponizing the tragic migration crisis in Ceuta for domestic political gain, arguing that mainstream EU leaders should instead show solidarity and cooperate with Spain.
skimming: A tragic mass migration attempt to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta resulted in at least 72 deaths, driven by social media misinformation and economic frustration.

Right-wing European leaders like Italy's Giorgia Meloni and Germany's Friedrich Merz exploited the crisis to posture for domestic audiences, despite their claims having little geographical or policy relevance to Ceuta.
The actual numbers of irregular border crossings into Europe have decreased by 40% in early 2026 due to better preventive strategies.
The author urges mainstream EU leaders to support Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and cooperate on migration challenges instead of using hyperbolic rhetoric.

title: The Guardian view on funerals: the law must change following Robert Bush’s crimes | Editorial
content: An undertaker’s trial has exposed a regulatory blind spot. The public, as well as trade bodies, should be involved in shaping reform There are few more vulnerable moments in life than the days before and after the loss of a loved one. The rituals of farewell surrounding a funeral matter deeply. Hence the horrified public reaction to the crimes of Robert Bush in Hull. Bush was sentenced last week to 20 years in prison for 67 offences including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial. When his business, Legacy Independent Funeral Services, was searched, police found multiple bodies decomposing on racks. Bush had returned the wrong ashes to families, stolen money donated to charities and spent more than £42,000 on holidays over 12 years. In court, relatives revealed the distress caused; David Gorbutt, who scattered a stranger’s ashes in place of his wife’s, described feeling “abused”. The Competition and Markets Authority proposed tighter regulation of the funeral industry in 2020. The independent inquiry into David Fuller – who abused the bodies of more than 100 women and girls in hospital mortuaries – included regulation of undertakers among its recommendations. Now, a year after that report was published, ministers have decided that they agree. New laws, which should be expected to include a licensing scheme, minimum standards and provision for inspections, are on the way. This is the right call. It is a peculiar blind spot in UK law that a service as sensitive and essential as that provided by undertakers is unregulated; the Scottish government, recognising this, introduced its own system last year. And while Bush’s case is by far the most extreme of several recent ones, he is not the only undertaker to have been jailed. Last year, another funeral director, Amie Upton, was banned from NHS mortuaries and maternity wards in Leeds after the BBC uncovered complaints about Florrie’s Army, a baby-loss service that she set up. Ms Upton has not been charged with any crime. But the Labour MP Mark Sewards has argued, rightly, that his constituents’ disturbing experiences with Florrie’s Army point to the need for new laws. An enhanced role for local government would be in keeping with the government’s devolution push, and would require funding. Trade organisations have proposed a model in which they would play a part alongside the Human Tissue Authority. But while all options should be looked at, regulation must not be mistaken for a panacea. As in other situations where a position of trust has been abused, opportunities to intervene in Hull appear to have been missed. About 65% of the more than 500,000 funerals that take place in the UK each year are handled by small, independent businesses. Regulation must be protective of them as well as of families who want to prepare bodies for cremation or burial themselves. Undertakers do a difficult job; those paying for their services are often extremely vulnerable. The likely increase in the cost of funerals, following tighter regulation, must also be taken seriously. Many people already struggle to afford them. It is vital to find out what the public, as well as the industry, want. It may be that laws concerning dead bodies require a wider review, as the Law Commission believes. But the priority must be to find an effective, proportionate way to prevent rogue operators from setting up funeral businesses, and to identify any who already have. Grieving people ought to be able to have confidence in those they entrust with the bodies of relatives. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: The horrific crimes of undertaker Robert Bush highlight a critical regulatory blind spot in the UK's funeral industry, necessitating urgent, balanced, and comprehensive legal reforms to protect vulnerable grieving families.
skimming: The conviction of Robert Bush for multiple offences, including preventing lawful burials, has exposed a severe lack of regulation in the UK funeral sector.
In response to these crimes and previous inquiry recommendations, the UK government is planning new laws to introduce licensing, minimum standards, and inspections.
While regulation is necessary, it must not be treated as a panacea, as past opportunities to intervene in cases of abuse were repeatedly missed.
Future regulatory frameworks must balance protecting vulnerable families with maintaining affordability and supporting small, independent funeral operators.
grammar: The sentence 'There are few more vulnerable moments in life than the days before and after the loss of a loved one' utilizes an existential 'there' construction combined with a comparative adjective structure ('few more... than...') to emphasize a universal human condition and set a solemn, empathetic premise for the argument.

title: The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it | Editorial
content: Devolution should finance transport, skills and industry, not become a rightwing contest to promise the largest tax giveaway That England is among the rich world’s most centralised countries underpins Andy Burnham’s critique of the economic history of the past 40 years. Only post-communist Europe deindustrialised as rapidly as Yorkshire and the Midlands did in the 1980s. Centralisation did not close every factory or pit, but left regions without the powers, finance or institutions to cushion the shock or build a resilient, replacement economy. Hence Mr Burnham’s radical and welcome plan to unbundle English government. There are three facets to his devolution programme. The first are the detailed and concrete proposals contained in a cabinet paper Mr Burnham released on Friday. This appears to be a blueprint to create a decentralised state organised around mayors as the key regional economic actors, while jointly governed pan-regional agencies could emerge, say for transport, energy, investment and industrial systems, that cross mayoral boundaries. Regions without mayors will get a chance to have one – or limit themselves to weaker powers. The second, outlined in the Guardian and later confirmed by No 10, is that mayors will be able to keep income-tax and business-rate revenues, with the forthcoming budget and spending review deciding on how much. Before entering No 10, Mr Burnham proposed a third pillar: a duty, modelled on Germany’s Basic Law, requiring English regions to pursue equivalent living conditions nationwide. Following this logic, a mayoral authority would receive a share of tax revenues and benefit when its economy and tax base grow. But the national government would continue redistributing resources so that poorer places can provide comparable services and possess meaningful investment capacity. Without such an equalisation measure, disparities would widen. One thinktank pointed out that if mayors received 2.5% of the 20p basic rate of income tax, London would get £2.3bn in 2026-27 while Hull and East Yorkshire would get £135m. Ben Houchen, the Tory mayor of Tees Valley, wants to turn devolved income-tax revenues into new powers to offer tax rebates. That mistakes a regional investment settlement for a tax-cutting competition: poorer places would forfeit the cash needed to rebuild transport links as well as skills and industrial capacity. What some rightwingers seek is to turn regional elections into tax-cutting auctions over who can return the most public money. But cash giveaways now would just mean the bill of the underinvestment would land later. England’s devolution map remains incomplete, but Mr Burnham wants to finish it. New mayors are due in Cumbria, and Cheshire and Warrington, in 2027, followed by ones in southern and eastern regions in 2028. The rest of the country will be asked to choose between mayoral strategic authorities with stronger powers or non-mayoral “foundation” bodies operating with more limited controls. A new Harvard Kennedy School and King’s College London paper, co-authored by the former Labour minister Ed Balls, argues that Britain’s weak productivity stems from persistent regional divides, with the gap between south-east England and the rest of the nation wider than that separating east and west Germany today. One reason this has not been tackled is that Britain has never had both No 10 and the Treasury committed to regional growth. Now it does. The country may finally discover what happens when the centre pulls in the same direction. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: England's highly centralized state has historically hindered regional economic resilience, and Andy Burnham's proposed devolution plan offers a viable path to address deep-seated regional productivity divides through mayoral empowerment and structured tax redistribution.
skimming: England's extreme centralization historically left regions vulnerable to rapid deindustrialization without local powers to recover.
Andy Burnham's devolution plan proposes a decentralized state structured around regional mayors, pan-regional agencies, and tax-revenue retention.
A critical pillar of the plan is a redistribution mechanism (inspired by Germany's Basic Law) to prevent widening disparities between wealthy and poorer regions.
The editorial warns against turning devolved tax powers into tax-cutting competitions, emphasizing that regional growth requires sustained public investment.
grammar: The sentence 'That England is among the rich world’s most centralised countries underpins Andy Burnham’s critique...' uses a noun clause ('That England is among...') as the grammatical subject of the main verb 'underpins'. title: The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics | Editorial
content: Funders have picked a damaging fight with scientists and the public. They should reconsider their plans The iconic Lovell telescope, housed at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire, has always expanded our view of the universe – from tracking the Sputnik launch in 1957 to its current contributions to the study of dark matter. It is now threatened with closure after it was announced that government funding will not continue past March 2028. The projected savings are just £2.8m a year. This is just the latest in a rolling package of cuts from the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) – which disperses government funding to particle, astro and nuclear physics, among other disciplines – aimed at saving about £160m over the next four years. The STFC has insisted that the measures are a result of cost overruns. That may be true, but it is hard not to see this as part of a larger shift in what kind of science the government funds and prioritises, and what areas it allows to wither. There is no doubt that physics is expensive. From telescopes to synchrotron beams, its instruments are increasingly large-scale and power-hungry. And scientists are not immune to the cost of living crisis. If households are feeling the pinch of electricity costs, just imagine getting the monthly bill for a particle accelerator. However, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), of which the STFC is a subsidiary, has just gone through a revamp of its funding model, one that clearly prioritises economic growth and measureable outcomes. Looking across the programmes cut, which include international collaborations with other telescope arrays and the Cern facility in Switzerland, many scientists believe that long-term, fundamental research is under specific threat. The UKRI and STFC have not helped the situation by badly misreading the politics. In a session at the House of Lords earlier this month, the UKRI chief, Ian Chapman, seemed surprised by the scientists’ “hyperbolic” reaction, and noted that they “feel that they have been cut” when, in fact, overall physics funding has increased. But scientists have reason to feel slighted when valued ongoing projects and collaborations – rather than future plans – are axed, and when what appear to be relatively small cost savings (the UKRI budget will be £10bn by 2030) fall on their shoulders. There are shades of the departed Starmer government in this saga: the UKRI wants to tell a big story about science funding going up, but instead is mired in a row over a fairly minor sum that has angered scientists and sections of the public. One does not have to be an astronomer to know that optics matter. The UKRI and STFC are technically arm’s‑length bodies, but it hasn’t escaped notice that the ministers who set its funding priorities, Liz Kendall and Patrick Vallance, are no longer in office, while Andy Burnham has abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. It would seem a good time for the current course to be reconsidered, whether by the funding councils or the new government itself. There is a conversation to be had about what research we fund with limited resources, and the balance between so-called blue sky projects and those expected to yield commercial returns. But when physicists warn that the UK could lose a “generation of scientists” to these cuts – in one of the few fields in which we can credibly claim to be world-leading – they should be heeded. It’s time to refocus, and look again. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: The editorial criticizes the UK government's short-sighted budget cuts to fundamental physics research, arguing that defunding iconic projects like the Lovell telescope damages scientific progress and political credibility.
skimming: The iconic Lovell telescope faces closure by 2028 due to a £2.8m annual funding cut, part of a larger £160m reduction by the STFC.
These cuts signal a shift in funding priorities away from long-term, fundamental research toward short-term economic growth and measurable outcomes.
The scientific community is deeply upset because ongoing, highly valued collaborations are being axed despite an overall increase in physics funding.
The author warns that the UK risks losing a generation of world-leading scientists unless the government and funding councils reconsider their course.
grammar: The sentence 'It is now threatened with closure after it was announced that...' features a double passive construction. The first 'it' refers to the telescope, while the second 'it' is a dummy pronoun acting as a placeholder for the delayed subject clause 'that government funding will not continue...'. This structure is common in formal writing to maintain objectivity.
